clue.text: Favourite knocking out United? Forest manager will take care of it

definitions.text: Forest manager will take care of it

indicators.note: knocking something out removes it, so a letter is taken away from the word

parts.note: a favourite is well liked
U is the standard abbreviation for United in team names

explanation.surface: A football fan's favourite side is knocked out, and someone else will look after things.
explanation.walkthrough: POPULAR loses its U. The definition is a whimsical description: a forester tends the trees in the woods.
explanation.definitionFit: A poplar is a tree, and trees are what a forester looks after.

clue.text: Endless depression over crude plagiarism

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: a pit is a hollow or depression in the ground
racy means risqué or crude

explanation.surface: Endless gloom follows the discovery of crude copying of someone's work.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'over' means above, putting the first piece on top of the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Piracy is the unauthorised copying of another's work, so it covers plagiarism of material.

clue.text: Gather leaves together with me

parts.note: surface reading: a gardener collecting fallen foliage; setter's reading: leaves are sheets of paper, and the speaker is an office fastener that holds them

explanation.walkthrough: Leaves suggests autumn raking, but leaves of paper are pages, and the speaker is a small wire stationery item.
explanation.definitionFit: This small bent wire is used to hold sheets of paper together in an office.

clue.text: Blunt, possibly reacts badly on set at first

indicators.note: done badly means done wrongly, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: at first points to the opening letter of the preceding word only

parts.note: first letter

explanation.surface: Someone blunt responds poorly on a film set from the start.
explanation.walkthrough: Blunt is Emily Blunt, the British film star; 'possibly' warns that she is just one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Emily Blunt is a performer in films, an example of the category, flagged by 'possibly'.

clue.text: What rugby ball might hit when it's 24-5

parts.note: 24 Across is TRAVERSE, and to traverse is to cross
5 Down is RAIL, and a rail is a bar

explanation.surface: A rugby score of 24-5 suggests a ball bouncing off the woodwork.
explanation.walkthrough: The score is really two cross-references: synonyms of the answers to 24 Across and 5 Down.
explanation.definitionFit: In rugby the horizontal beam between the posts is the crossbar, which a kick at goal can strike.

clue.text: Scoff starters of radicchio and linguine when touring Italy

indicators.note: touring means travelling round, so the kept letters go around the country letter
starters are the opening items, so the first letter of each word is kept

parts.note: first letters of the three words
I is the international vehicle code for Italy

explanation.surface: A traveller in Italy eats radicchio and linguine for starters.
explanation.walkthrough: Scoff looks like British slang for eating greedily, matching the food, but here it means to jeer.
explanation.definitionFit: To rail is to complain or protest bitterly, close to scoffing at or mocking something.

clue.text: Cook also cut tuna and fruit

indicators.note: cut means shortened, so the word loses its final letter
to cook something is to work it up or alter it, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the word without its last letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: A chef prepares sliced tuna along with some fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cook' looks like a person in the kitchen; it is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A sultana is a dried seedless grape, a type of dried fruit.

clue.text: Lively British board game

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for British
Risk is a board game of world conquest

explanation.surface: An energetic British board game.
explanation.definitionFit: Brisk means active and energetic, so it is a synonym of lively.

clue.text: Cavalier maybe, run out close to wary top celebrities

parts.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for run
O is a cricket scorecard abbreviation for out

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so only its last letter is kept

parts.note: last letter
the A-list are the most famous celebrities

explanation.surface: A careless cricketer is run out, which puts the watching celebrities on their guard.
explanation.walkthrough: Cavaliers were supporters of King Charles I in the English Civil War; 'maybe' marks it as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: A Cavalier fought for the king in the English Civil War, so was a supporter of the monarchy.

clue.text: Good name of seller backed by Gumtree regularly

parts.note: a sales rep sells goods

indicators.note: regularly means at fixed intervals, so every other letter of the tree word is kept

parts.note: second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: A trader on Gumtree, the online classifieds site, relies on a good name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backed by' here means followed by: the seller comes first and the selected letters follow.
explanation.definitionFit: Repute is reputation, the standing a person has with others, which is what a good name means.

clue.text: Victor, current dodgy ally in crime

parts.note: V is Victor in the NATO phonetic alphabet

indicators.note: something dodgy is unreliable and not straight, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: I is the symbol for electric current
the two words supply the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone named Victor teams up with a shady accomplice in a criminal scheme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a link to 'crime' but belongs to the letters being rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Villainy is wicked or criminal behaviour, so it stands for crime as an uncountable noun.

clue.text: Platitudes from Truss? I'm shocked!

indicators.note: shocked suggests being jolted and thrown into disorder, so the letters are mixed up

parts.note: taken as written, ignoring punctuation

explanation.surface: Someone is appalled by the empty phrases of Liz Truss, the short-lived British Prime Minister.
explanation.definitionFit: A truism is a self-evident, trite statement, so truisms are platitudes.

clue.text: Vessel from Spooner's distant Irish county

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words, so two initial sounds trade places

parts.note: distant is far, and Kerry is a county in south-west Ireland; swapping their opening sounds gives the spoken answer

explanation.surface: A boat comes from a remote part of Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: Swapping the opening sounds of FAR KERRY gives CAR FERRY.
explanation.definitionFit: A car ferry is a ship that carries vehicles, so it is a type of vessel.

clue.text: Knave chased by a large wild dog

parts.note: the knave is the jack in a pack of cards
taken as written
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: A villain is pursued by a big wild dog.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chased by' means followed by, so the knave comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: The jackal is a wild canine of Africa and Asia, so it is an example of a wild dog.

clue.text: Act right in gym class

indicators.note: in places one element inside another, so the side letter goes within the lesson words

parts.note: PE is physical education, gym lessons at school
a form is a class in a British school
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A pupil behaves well in a school gym lesson.
explanation.walkthrough: The right-hand letter sits between the gym and class pieces. A form is a school class or year group in British usage.
explanation.definitionFit: To perform is to act on stage, so the two verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Novel sales rise with Mel B book

indicators.note: novel means new and different, so these letters take a fresh order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A novel's sales climb after a Spice Girl gets involved with the book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like the definition but is the anagram signal; the definition is 'book' at the end. Mel B is a member of the Spice Girls pop group.
explanation.definitionFit: Les Misérables is Victor Hugo's celebrated novel, an example of a book.

clue.text: Pork pie at hand, pass the time lazily

parts.note: pork pie is cockney rhyming slang for lie
around means nearby, close at hand

explanation.surface: With a pork pie within reach, someone idles the hours away.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockney rhyming slang uses a rhyming phrase for a word: pork pie (often 'porky') means lie.
explanation.definitionFit: To lie around is an idiom for lounging idly, doing nothing in particular.

clue.text: Generous worker supporting sailor and German

indicators.note: in a down clue a support sits underneath, so this piece is placed below the others

parts.note: AB is an able seaman
und is the German word for and
a worker ant

explanation.surface: A generous employee backs up a seaman and a German colleague.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'supporting' means placed below, so the worker comes last.
explanation.definitionFit: Abundant means plentiful or ample, as a generous helping is.

clue.text: First tough problem, zero Fahrenheit inside immersion heater!

parts.note: baptism is often by immersion in water
zero looks like the letter O

indicators.note: inside means placed within, so a pair of letters sits between the other parts

parts.note: a fire heats a room
F is the abbreviation for Fahrenheit

explanation.surface: The first snag of a new home: the immersion heater has stopped working and the water is freezing.
explanation.walkthrough: An immersion heater is a British domestic water heater; here it splits into two words, with the two letters going between them.
explanation.definitionFit: A baptism of fire is a hard initial experience, an idiom for being tested at the very start.

clue.text: Nurse is changing covers

indicators.note: changing means altering, so the letters move into a different order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A nurse is changing bed covers on the ward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Covers' reads as bedclothes but is a verb, meaning provides insurance for.
explanation.definitionFit: To cover something is to protect it with insurance, so covers and insures are synonyms.

clue.text: Account from one knight, say

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
N is the chess notation for knight
to voice is to say

explanation.surface: A knight gives his version of events.
explanation.definitionFit: An invoice is a bill, and account is another word for a bill sent to a customer.

clue.text: Divide by sixty-one at the end? Tough

parts.note: to sever is to cut apart

indicators.note: at the end points to the final letter of the number word only

parts.note: last letter

explanation.surface: Dividing by sixty-one makes for a hard sum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Divide by' reads as arithmetic, but 'by' only means next to.
explanation.definitionFit: Severe means harsh or demanding, so it is a synonym of tough.

clue.text: Most agreeable French resort — sunlit, deserted

parts.note: Nice is a resort on the French Riviera

indicators.note: deserted means emptied, so the middle of the word is cleared and only its ends remain

parts.note: first and last letters

explanation.surface: A sunny French resort with empty streets would be most pleasant.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicest is the superlative of nice, meaning most pleasant, matching the superlative in the definition.

clue.text: Bad-mannered person beginning to criticise cast

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter, which is all that is kept

parts.note: first letter
to cast is to throw

explanation.surface: A rude person starts to criticise the actors in a play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cast' suggests actors in a production but is the verb to throw.
explanation.definitionFit: A churl is a rude, surly, ill-bred person.

clue.text: Tense Republican opposed Ford

parts.note: T is the grammatical abbreviation for tense
R is the abbreviation for Republican
averse means opposed or hostile to

explanation.surface: A tense Republican politician stood against President Ford.
explanation.walkthrough: Ford looks like the Republican president Gerald Ford, but here it is a verb: to cross a river.
explanation.definitionFit: To ford is to cross a river by wading, and to traverse is likewise to go across.

clue.text: Clasp and ring for writer of 15 Across

parts.note: to clasp is to embrace
O is ring-shaped

explanation.surface: An embrace and a ring are offered for the author of a famous novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Victor Hugo, the French author, wrote Les Misérables, the answer at 15 Across.

clue.text: Greenish-blue, strange exterior to independent school here?

parts.note: aqua is a greenish-blue colour

indicators.note: something exterior to another lies around its outside, so one part wraps the other

parts.note: rum is British slang for odd or strange
I is the abbreviation for independent

explanation.surface: A pupil wonders about a strange blue-green private school building.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Independent school' reads as a private school, but only 'independent' gives a letter; 'school' belongs to the definition, meaning a school of fish.
explanation.definitionFit: An aquarium is a tank where fish are kept, so a school of fish might be found swimming in it.

clue.text: Guess number

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to reckon or work out
second meaning: a numeral or digit

explanation.walkthrough: The two words read as a quiz instruction, but each is a separate meaning of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means to reckon or suppose; as a noun it is a written digit.

clue.text: Discuss job and work after utter silence

parts.note: to utter is to speak
sh is the call for silence
op is short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: Colleagues talk about a job and get to work after a hushed pause.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' puts the work last, following the other two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: To talk shop is an idiom for discussing one's work, especially in social settings.

clue.text: On the radio, Gong and Snoop

indicators.note: a radio broadcast is heard rather than seen, so the word is judged by its sound

parts.note: gong is British slang for a medal or decoration

explanation.surface: A radio programme features a gong and the rapper Snoop Dogg.
explanation.walkthrough: Gong is informal British for a medal or honour.
explanation.definitionFit: To snoop is to pry into others' affairs, close in sense to interfering in them.
